title: Streaming Speech-to-Speech — Moshi, Hibiki, and Full-Duplex Dialogue

questions.question: A system listens while it speaks and can react to interruptions. Which interaction mode describes this?
options: One-way text-to-speech
Turn-by-turn waveform conversion
Full-duplex speech-to-speech
Offline speech recognition
questions.explanation: Full-duplex speech-to-speech keeps incoming and outgoing audio active at the same time, so the system can listen while responding. One-way TTS waits for text and emits speech; it does not continuously listen for an interruption.

questions.question: What are the three parallel streams in the lesson’s Moshi architecture?
options: Source audio, translated words, and a mel filterbank
Mimi audio, VAD events, and transcript timestamps
User audio, Moshi audio, and Moshi text
User text, target waveform, and speaker embeddings
questions.explanation: Moshi processes user Mimi audio, its own generated Mimi audio, and a text inner-monologue stream in parallel. VAD and timestamps are not the three streams in the model’s joint audio-text architecture.

questions.question: What does the depth transformer predict within each 80 ms frame?
options: The dependent codec codebooks in sequence
Only the user transcript and its timestamps
The next turn boundary from silence duration
All eight codebooks independently at once
questions.explanation: Within each 80 ms frame, codebooks depend on earlier codebooks, so a small depth transformer predicts them sequentially. Parallel independent prediction ignores the inter-codebook dependencies the depth transformer is designed to model.

questions.question: Why emit inner-monologue text alongside Moshi audio?
options: It prevents the user from speaking during assistant output
It supports semantic coherence and provides transcripts
It converts every user utterance into an external LM prompt
It removes the need for an audio codec entirely
questions.explanation: Text tokens make the model’s intended utterance explicit, improving semantic coherence and providing a transcript alongside generated audio. The text stream does not replace Mimi: the model still consumes and generates codec audio streams.

questions.question: A voice companion must respond naturally at very low latency and handle interruptions without tool calls. Which option best fits?
options: Moshi’s full-duplex dialogue architecture
Sesame CSM’s context-conditioned TTS
Hibiki’s speech-translation model
A cascaded ASR, LLM, and TTS pipeline
questions.explanation: Moshi’s parallel input-output streams support low-latency dialogue and interruption handling, which fits a voice companion without tool use. A pipeline supports tools, but its serial stages add latency and are not the lesson’s lowest-latency full-duplex design.

questions.question: A deployment needs an assistant to call a weather tool while speaking. What architecture guidance does the lesson give?
options: Use a tool-capable pipeline or add a separate LLM path
Assume Moshi’s dialogue model already supports tool calls
Use Hibiki because translation enables function execution
Replace all Mimi tokens with tool-call JSON
questions.explanation: The lesson says Moshi is a dialogue model rather than an agent framework; tool use needs a pipeline or a separate LLM path. The source explicitly says tool calling is not trained into Moshi, so a tool-capable path must be added.
